content: The work titled Experiments on Plant Hybridization, authored by Gregor Mendel in 1865, was the culmination of years of meticulous research into the inheritance of genetic traits in pea plants. Mendel presented his findings to the Natural History Society of Brünn in Bohemia during meetings held on February 8 and March 8 of that year. His paper was subsequently published in the Proceedings of the Natural History Society in 1866. In his study, Mendel analyzed seven distinct traits in pea plants, which included: 1. The color and texture of the seeds (either gray and round or white and wrinkled). 2. The color of the cotyledons (yellow or green). 3. The color of the flowers (white or violet). 4. The shape of the pods (full or constricted). 5. The color of the unripe pods (yellow or green). 6. The position of the flowers and pods on the stems. 7. The height of the plants (short or tall). Through his experiments, Mendel discovered that one trait would consistently dominate over its recessive counterpart. This principle, later termed Mendelian inheritance or Mendelian genetics, challenged the prevailing theory of blending inheritance at the time. Despite the groundbreaking nature of his work, Mendel's research initially received little attention from the scientific community and was largely forgotten. It was not until the early 20th century that his findings were rediscovered and became foundational to the modern synthesis of genetics. In the 20th century, the statistician R.A. Fisher applied a chi-square test to Mendel's data and concluded that the results were improbably close to the predicted ratios. Fisher suggested that the data might have been adjusted, either intentionally or unconsciously, to align with Mendel's hypothesis. However, subsequent researchers have criticized Fisher's analysis, offering alternative statistical and botanical explanations for Mendel's results. It is also plausible that Mendel's data appeared too perfect because he selectively reported the most representative subset of his experiments, as he himself acknowledged in his paper.
